newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to cut spending to 15.5 pct of GDP in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Russia to cut spending to 15.5 pct of GDP in 1998.

text.p: Russia's draft 1998 budget sets spending at 15.5 percent of gross domestic product, down from 19.4 percent in the 1997 budget, First Deputy Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin said on Wednesday.
But the government plans to reduce budgeted spending this year to 15.6 percent of GDP, cutting spending on most items by half, because of a shortfall in revenues, he told a news conference.
Under the 1997 budget law the government must propose a sequester bill, or spending cuts, if revenues fall below 90 percent of planned levels in any quarter.
Last month government officials said Russia had met only 49 percent of the tax receipts target in the first quarter.
Kudrin said the reduction in spending would help Russia transfer to a new tax code, which provides for fewer taxes and a lower tax take.
"This corresponds to our strategic goal of cutting government spending and its part in the GDP and gradually lowering the tax burden," he said.
The State Duma lower house of parliament will debate the government's sequester plans on May 21.
Kudrin blamed the tax shortfall partly on the Duma's failure to approve a number of tax laws, revenues from which were included in the budget.
He said the failure to pass a law requiring taxes to be paid before wages had cost the government between 33 to 55 trillion roubles.

Failure to approve cuts in privileges in paying value-added tax had cost the government 15 trillion roubles and failure to approve a tax on hard currency sales by individuals had cost 2.3 trillion roubles.

The goverment plans to cut planned spending by 105 trillion roubles, cutting most budget items by 55 percent. Some priority articles, such as funding supplies to the Far North, financing the coal industry and defence spending, will be cut by only 30 percent, Kudrin said.
